title: Why Broken Promises Crash Your Self-Control
description:
Documentary case briefing on Why Broken Promises — Not Weak Willpower — Crash the measured neural protocol, grounded in Celeste Kidd (2013) (Cognition). Empirical findings show that in Walter Mischel's classic Stanford paradigm, preschoolers sat alone for up to 15 minutes facing one marshmallow now or two if they waited until the researcher returned.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how nucleus accumbens, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that in 2013, Celeste Kidd tested 28 children aged 3 to 5 by first promising fancy art supplies and either delivering them or apologizing empty-handed before running the measured neural protocol.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Celeste Kidd, Holly Palmeri, Richard N. Aslin (2013). Rational snacking: Young children’s decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2012.08.004
- Walter Mischel, Ebbe B. Ebbesen, Antonette Raskoff Zeiss (1972). Cognitive and attentional mechanisms in delay of gratification. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0032198
- Tyler W. Watts, Greg J. Duncan, Haonan Quan (2018). Revisiting the Marshmallow Test: A Conceptual Replication Investigating Links Between Early Delay of Gratification and Later Outcomes. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797618761661

AI Disclosure: Visuals and voice synthesis in this documentary were generated with AI tools to illustrate peer-reviewed neuroscience findings.
debate_question: When your habits slip at night, is the real culprit weak willpower — or broken self-trust?
offcenter_creator_bet: My bet: willpower is mostly self-trust.
